title: Living water (John 4:7–15)
hook: whoever drinks the water I give shall not thirst for ever

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Augustine: he must increase, but I must decrease. Your line was glad to stand near. Who got the credit from you? Day five hundred. Five hundred days on the path.

Noon in Samaria. About the sixth hour, John says. Jesus is tired from the road and sits down by Jacob's well, while his disciples go into the town to buy food. A woman of Samaria comes out with her jar to draw water. John adds a note that explains the distance between them: the Jews do not communicate with the Samaritans. A Jewish man, a Samaritan woman, and a well between them. And then he speaks to her, and his first words are a request.
screen: `NOON AT JACOB'S WELL.` → `A WOMAN COMES TO DRAW WATER.` → `A TIRED STRANGER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: He says: "Give me to drink." In John's telling, the one with the gift begins by asking. She's startled. How do you, a Jew, ask a drink of me, a Samaritan woman? And he answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "If thou didst know the gift of God, and who he is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou perhaps wouldst have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water." Living water. Living water can mean plain running water: a spring, a stream, water that moves, not still water in a cistern. She takes him that way, literally and very practically. Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well? He doesn't argue about Jacob. He points at the bucket. Whoever drinks this water will be thirsty again. Tomorrow at noon she'll be back with the jar. But, he says, "he that shall drink of the water that I will give him, shall not thirst for ever." It becomes a spring inside, welling up into everlasting life. And she answers like anyone carrying a heavy jar: Sir, give me this water, so I don't have to keep coming here. She still thinks it's about the walk to the well. Early in its teaching on prayer, the Catechism turns to this scene. It says that Jesus thirsts, and his asking comes from the depth of God's desire for us. Prayer, it says, whether we know it or not, is the meeting of God's thirst with ours. The one who began by asking for a drink is the one who has the water.
screen: `GIVE ME TO DRINK.` · `LIVING WATER: RUNNING WATER.` · `THIS WATER, THIRSTY AGAIN.` · `GOD'S THIRST MEETS OURS.` · then, large: `SHALL NOT THIRST FOR EVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drink water slowly and pray. Get a glass of water if you can. Settle, and breathe. Lift the glass and feel its weight. Take one slow sip, and notice the cool of it going down. Then another. Think of the thirst underneath this one, if there is one: something you keep going back to the well for, that never quite fills. If you pray, you can ask, as she did, give me this water. If you don't, just drink slowly and pay attention to being thirsty and being given something. The bell holds the time.
Living water. A phrase for running spring water; in John, the gift Jesus offers at Jacob's well that ends thirst for ever. Today's word.
Your line: never thirst. Today, every time you drink water, let it remind you of the one who asked first. Day five hundred.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the woman at the well on the Third Sunday of Lent in Year A, often with adults preparing for baptism at Easter, and the Catechism turns to this scene early in its teaching on prayer.

original.note: Greek: living water (John 4:10), a phrase that can mean running, spring water.

trapdoor: what you thought: living water is a poetic phrase Jesus made up.
what it means: a phrase that can mean plain running water, which Jesus fills with a new meaning: a spring of everlasting life.
what a scholar hears: hydōr zōn can mean flowing water; the Catechism (2560) reads the scene as God's thirst meeting ours in prayer.

notes: Day 500 milestone mentioned briefly in the review.
'Nobody goes to the well at noon' and the woman's coming alone as significant: a common reading, not stated in the text. Softened to scene-setting; confirm.
CCC 2560 paraphrased (Jesus thirsts; his asking arises from God's desire for us; prayer is the encounter of God's thirst with ours). Confirm.
Jewish–Samaritan relations described as 'a long and bitter history; they didn't share cups' (John 4:9). Confirm the framing is fair to both.
Third Sunday of Lent, Year A, used with the Scrutinies for the elect. Confirm.

Editor review (483-500 pass): cut the unsourced 'nobody goes to the well at noon / she comes alone' trope, 'the hottest part of the day' and 'men didn't speak to women'; the Jewish-Samaritan note now follows John 4:9; 'God begins by asking' no longer states belief as fact; 'living water meant running water' softened to 'can mean'; the 'shall not thirst for ever' quote now matches the Douay's lowercase 'but' and its verse (4:13); 'opens its teaching on prayer' softened.
